extraction.name: MATH
extraction.description: A dataset of 12,500 challenging competition mathematics problems from high school math competitions (AMC 10, AMC 12, AIME, etc.) with full step-by-step solutions. Problems span seven subjects (Prealgebra, Algebra, Number Theory, Counting and Probability, Geometry, Intermediate Algebra, and Precalculus) and are tagged by difficulty from 1 to 5.
extraction.creator: Dan Hendrycks, Collin Burns, Saurav Kadavath, Akul Arora, Steven Basart, Eric Tang, Dawn Song, Jacob Steinhardt
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The MATH dataset consists of 12,500 problems from mathematics competitions including the AMC 10, AMC 12, AIME, and more, collected from aops.com/community/c3158_usa_contests. These competitions span decades and assess the mathematical problem-solving ability of the best young mathematical talent in the United States. Each problem has a step-by-step solution and a final boxed answer. The AMPS pretraining dataset contains over 100,000 problems from Khan Academy exercises (693 exercise types) and approximately 5 million problems generated from 100 manually designed Mathematica scripts covering various mathematical topics.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw data consists of mathematics competition problems from AMC 10, AMC 12, AIME and other competitions spanning decades, Khan Academy exercises covering K-12 mathematics through multivariable calculus, and algorithmically generated problems from Mathematica scripts. Problems and solutions are formatted using LaTeX and the Asymptote vector graphics language for mathematical figures.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Problems were collected from mathematics competitions including AMC 10, AMC 12, AIME, and others from aops.com/community/c3158_usa_contests. Each problem includes a full step-by-step solution and final boxed answer. Problems are categorized by subject (7 subjects: Prealgebra, Algebra, Number Theory, Counting and Probability, Geometry, Intermediate Algebra, and Precalculus) and difficulty level (1-5 following AoPS standards). Problems and solutions are formatted using LaTeX and Asymptote vector graphics language with consistent formatting rules for answers.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Human-level performance was evaluated by having university students solve 20 randomly sampled problems with 1 hour time limit and hand calculations. Results ranged from 40% (student who doesn't like mathematics) to 90% (three-time IMO gold medalist). Expert-level performance is theoretically 100% given enough time.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: University students with varying levels of mathematical ability and interest, ranging from students who don't like mathematics to IMO gold medalists
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Mathematica scripts were used to generate approximately 5 million problems with step-by-step solutions. 100 hand-designed Mathematica scripts were created covering various mathematics topics, with 37 scripts generating full step-by-step LaTeX solutions in addition to final answers.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset is limited to high school mathematics competition problems from specific sources (AMC 10, AMC 12, AIME). Problems are categorized by difficulty levels 1-5 and span seven subjects. The dataset requires consistent LaTeX formatting and uses the Asymptote language for figures. Human-level performance varies significantly (40% for a CS PhD student who doesn't like math to 90% for a three-time IMO gold medalist), indicating the dataset can be challenging for humans as well.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset has implications for academic integrity, as achieving 40% accuracy on homework problems could enable cheating. The work aims to advance mathematical problem-solving capabilities in AI, which could have broad applications given the domain-generality of mathematics across sciences and intellectual endeavors.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The MATH dataset is designed for benchmarking mathematical problem-solving ability in machine learning models. The dataset includes 7,500 training problems and 5,000 test problems. The AMPS pretraining dataset (containing Khan Academy and Mathematica-generated problems) is used for pretraining models before fine-tuning on MATH. Models are trained to generate both final answers and step-by-step solutions.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: During pretraining, Khan Academy data was upsampled by a factor of 5 and Mathematica data was downsampled by a factor of 2 to account for the large difference in dataset sizes. During fine-tuning, models were trained with an equal mix of sequences containing only final answers and sequences containing full step-by-step solutions.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Problems and solutions were consistently formatted using LaTeX and the Asymptote vector graphics language. Final boxed answers were forced to follow consistent formatting rules including: probabilities expressed as simplified fractions, matrix entry fractions encoded with x/y while other fractions encoded with \frac{x}{y}, coefficients encoded without multiplication symbols, expressions with multiple variables in alphabetical order, polynomials in decreasing degree order. Different equivalent encodings were treated as the same (e.g., different fraction formats, parenthesis encodings, spaces ignored, equivalent number representations). Units could be included or omitted from answers.

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: To measure the problem-solving ability of machine learning models, we introduce the MATH dataset, which consists of 12,500 problems from high school math competitions... rai:dataManipulationProtocol.evidence: During pretraining, we upsample Khan Academy data by a factor of 5 and we downsample Mathematica by a factor of 2 to account for the large difference in dataset sizes... For fine-tuning we use the same batch size and weight decay as in pretraining... if hPi is the problem statement, we train with an equal mix of "hPi Final Answer: <Answer>" and "hPi Full Solution: <Step-by-Step Solution>" sequences.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: Problems and solutions are consistently formatted using LATEX and the Asymptote vector graphics language... To assess models using exact match, we force the final boxed answers to follow consistent formatting rules. Specifically, probabilities are expressed as simplified fractions. Moreover, matrix entry fractions are encoded with x/y, while all other fractions are consistently encoded with the \frac{x}{y} command. Coefficients are encoded without a multiplication symbol (e.g. 5x not 5*x). Expressions with multiple variables are entered in alphabetical order; polynomials are expressed in decreasing degree order.
